meanings.note: An affirmative response. Here it introduces his answer to the camera.
Unstressed ja can mark shared or apparent knowledge; that use is different from an ordinary yes.
Subject pronoun referring to the speaker; always written lowercase except at the start of a sentence.
Links a subject to a name, description or location. The present forms are irregular.
Used with certain verbs to form a compound past; the lesson uses it as a main verb.
The new supermarket employee speaking in this taster. This is his name, not a vocabulary phrase.
Refers to the current day. A time expression may begin a German statement, followed by the finite verb.
Marks the speaker as possessor. Its ending follows the gender, number and case of the following noun, not the gender of the speaker.
An ordinal word. In mein erster Tag the ending -er marks masculine nominative singular after the uninflected possessive mein.
Can refer to a calendar day or the daylight part of it. Here: the first day in a job.
A location near the speaker or the place currently under discussion. In this interview it means this workplace.
The definite article changes with gender, number and case. Die before anderen is accusative plural, not feminine singular.
With a definite article, refers to other people or things already understood. Die anderen here means the other staff.
Can also accompany a noun, as in eine andere Arbeit.

examples.trans: I am looking for another job.

meanings.en: to know a person or thing
meanings.note: Takes an accusative object. For knowing a fact or an answer, wissen is usually the relevant verb.

examples.text: Ich kenne die anderen noch nicht.
examples.trans: I do not know the others yet.

meanings.note: In noch nicht, something has not happened up to now.
Can also describe a state continuing: Ich bin noch hier.

examples.trans: I do not know him yet.

meanings.note: Negates a statement or part of one. In noch nicht so gut it qualifies how well he knows the others.

examples.trans: I do not know her yet.

meanings.note: Specifies degree before an adjective or adverb: nicht so gut means not so well.
Can refer to a manner of doing something.

examples.text: Ich kenne ihn nicht so gut.
examples.trans: I do not know him that well.

meanings.note: Used adverbially without an ending to describe how well he knows people.
As an adjective before a noun, takes an appropriate ending: ein guter Tag.
A coordinating conjunction introducing a contrast. It does not itself occupy the first position of the clause that follows.

examples.text: Ich bin neu, aber ich kenne ihn.
examples.trans: I am new, but I know him.

meanings.note: Here starts um … zu + infinitive, explaining a purpose. This is not the prepositional sense around, and does not itself govern a noun case here.

examples.text: Ich bin hier, um zu arbeiten.
Ich komme, um dich zu sehen.
examples.trans: I am coming to see you.

um.governs: Purpose clause: um … zu + infinitive; understood actor normally shared with the main clause.

meanings.note: Freunde finden means to make friends. The plural Freunde in this lesson does not specify one individual friend.
Singular mein Freund can mean my boyfriend, depending on the relationship and context.

examples.trans: I would like to make friends.

meanings.note: Here marks the infinitive in a purpose clause. It is not the dative preposition used before a destination or person.

examples.text: Ich habe Zeit, um zu lesen.
Ich bin hier, um Geld zu verdienen.
examples.trans: I am here to earn money.

zu.governs: Infinitive marker in um … zu; no noun case in this use.

meanings.note: Discover or come upon a person, thing or solution.
Freunde finden is idiomatic; English normally uses make rather than find.
Usually a mass noun in this general sense; German does not use an indefinite article in Geld verdienen.
The plural Gelder is used for particular sums, allocations or funds, rather than ordinary coins counted one by one.

examples.text: Das Geld ist für die Miete.
examples.trans: The money is for the rent.

meanings.note: Receive money for work.
Be worthy of something: Du verdienst eine Pause.
An informal farewell. Added as the lesson closing, not claimed as speech from the original excerpt.
